articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities.

These designations aim to disrupt the financial networks supporting illicit drug trafficking and terrorist organizations globally. The specific individuals and entities targeted were not immediately detailed in the initial announcement but are expected to be added to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List.
This action underscores the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to combating international criminal and terrorist networks through financial sanctions.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Sanctions List
body: OFAC issued an update to its Iran designations on November 9, 2026. This action signifies ongoing adjustments to the U.S. sanctions regime against Iran.
Details of the specific changes, including any new additions or modifications to existing listings, were not immediately provided but are part of the continuous effort to address Iran's activities.
The update reinforces the comprehensive nature of U.S. sanctions targeting various sectors and individuals associated with the Iranian government and its proxies.

articles.headline: New Iran-Related Designations Announced by OFAC
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026. This action targets additional entities and individuals connected to Iran's illicit activities.
These designations are part of the broader U.S. strategy to exert economic pressure on Iran and its support networks.
Further information regarding the specific targets and the implications of these designations is anticipated to be released by OFAC.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber and Transnational Criminal Organizations, Issues Cuba Sanctions
body: On November 5, 2026, OFAC announced designations targeting cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations, alongside new Cuba designations and the publication of a Cuba-related determination.

This action includes sanctioning one Chinese Mainland company and six Hong Kong companies for their alleged involvement in cyber-enabled fraud, money laundering, and human trafficking, purportedly linked to the Prince Group transnational criminal organization. The designations also target Malaysian national Chui Kok Wa, identified as the leader of a Madagascar-based scam network.
The Cuba-related actions further restrict financial interactions with the island nation, aligning with the U.S. government's policy to address human rights and democratic concerns.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran-Related Designations, Amends Venezuela General License
body: OFAC announced new Iran-related designations on November 4, 2026, along with updates to certain Iran-related listings and the publication of an Iran-related OFAC Alert.
Additionally, an amended Venezuela-related General License and a Frequently Asked Question were issued, indicating adjustments to the U.S. sanctions policy concerning Venezuela.
These actions reflect the U.S. government's dynamic approach to sanctions, adapting to evolving geopolitical circumstances and illicit activities in both regions.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Iran-Related General License
body: On October 29, 2026, OFAC issued an amended Iran-related General License. This amendment signifies a modification to existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.

General Licenses are often issued to permit specific activities that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs, typically to facilitate humanitarian aid, certain types of trade, or other policy objectives.
The details of the amendment would clarify the scope of permitted activities and any new conditions or restrictions.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Sanctions on North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: OFAC announced new designations targeting North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo on October 28, 2026. These actions aim to counter illicit activities and human rights abuses in both regions.
The designations against North Korea are likely related to its weapons of mass destruction programs and other destabilizing actions.
Sanctions concerning the Democratic Republic of the Congo typically address corruption, human rights violations, and conflict minerals, seeking to promote stability and accountability.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting
body: On October 26, 2026, OFAC issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC.
These amendments provide updated guidance and clarification for financial institutions and other entities on their compliance obligations under OFAC regulations.
The revised FAQs are crucial for ensuring proper adherence to sanctions programs and accurate reporting of blocked or rejected transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran, Russia General Licenses; Removes Belarus, North Korea Designations
body: On October 21, 2026, OFAC announced new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses, alongside the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea.

The issuance of new General Licenses for Iran and Russia indicates specific authorizations for transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, potentially easing restrictions in certain areas or for particular activities.

The removal of designations for Belarus and North Korea suggests a re-evaluation of sanctions targets in those regions, which could be due to policy shifts or changes in the behavior of the delisted entities.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC
body: Bank of America, N.A. has been assessed a civil monetary penalty of $11,662,930 by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC).

This penalty is in addition to a $750 million civil money penalty imposed by the OCC for deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act compliance program and failure to timely file suspicious activity reports.

The OCC stated that Bank of America's BSA/AML compliance program was deficient and ineffective, leading to a failure to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions and the late filing of numerous suspicious activity reports.

articles.headline: BIS Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced that, as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the State Department's U.S. Munitions List.
This deregulatory action aims to align export controls on suppressors with those already applied to firearms, easing compliance burdens on the firearms industry while maintaining national security.

Under this new rule, suppressors will be added to the Commerce Control List (CCL), and a license will be required for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers, with existing license exceptions for firearms also applicable to suppressors.

articles.headline: US Blocks Imports from Chinese Genomics Firms BGI Group, BGI Genomics, and MGI Tech Over Xinjiang Forced Labor Allegations
body: The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has added Chinese genomics companies BGI Group, BGI Genomics, and MGI Tech to the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA) Entity List.

This action effectively bars their goods from the U.S. market over alleged links to forced labor and the tracking of persecuted minorities in Xinjiang. The DHS stated that these companies 'helped collect genetic material used to track persecuted ethnic minorities, including people subjected to forced labor.'
The import ban follows a proposal by the U.S. Treasury Department to restrict U.S. investment in Chinese biotechnology, further widening U.S. trade controls into life sciences.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
